html:
Two inscriptions in a small rock-cut temple, the Chaturbhuj temple, inside Gwalior Fort in central India, dated to 876 CE. They contain one of the oldest dated uses of a written zero as a digit in a place-value number.

The temple was made by Alla, an official under the Gurjara-Pratihara kings. The texts record gifts of land and flowers to the temple. One gives a garden 270 hastas long, and a daily gift of 50 garlands; the "0" in each is a small circle, as zero is still written today.

The idea of zero as a number was older. Brahmagupta set rules for computing with it in his Brahmasphutasiddhanta of 628, and the Bakhshali manuscript uses a dot for zero. But the Gwalior stones are firmly dated, so they are a key witness. By then the system had already reached Baghdad, from where the Hindu-Arabic numerals passed to Europe.
sum: Two inscriptions in a small rock-cut temple, the Chaturbhuj temple, inside Gwalior Fort in central India, dated to 876 CE. They contain one of the oldest dated uses of a written zero as a digit in a place-value number.
